lead: Every engine is described with a fixed set of words: bore, stroke, crank radius, top and bottom dead centre, swept volume, clearance volume, compression ratio, piston speed and mean effective pressure. Every later calculation of power and efficiency is built from them. The same engine has a fixed set of parts, each with one job and a material chosen for that job. This chapter gives both lists, so later chapters can use the words and the parts without defining them again.
prereq: You need the reciprocating layout from history and classification of IC engines.

blocks.text: These terms describe one cylinder. Figure 1.2.1 marks each of them on the engine of the worked example.

items: Bore (d): the inside diameter of the cylinder, in mm.
Stroke (L): the distance the piston travels between its two end positions. The crank pin moves on a circle of radius a, the crank radius, so L = 2a.
Top dead centre (TDC): the piston position nearest the cylinder head, where the cylinder volume is smallest. Bottom dead centre (BDC): the position farthest from it, where the volume is largest.
Swept volume (Vs): the volume the piston sweeps from TDC to BDC. Engine displacement is Vs times the number of cylinders.
Clearance volume (Vc): the volume left above the piston at TDC; it holds the combustion chamber.
Compression ratio (r): the cylinder volume at BDC divided by the volume at TDC.
Connecting rod ratio: rod length l divided by crank radius a, usually 3.5 to 4.5 in car engines.

blocks.where: d is the bore and L the stroke in the same unit; centimetres give cm³.

blocks.text: r = (Vs + Vc)/Vc. Here r is a pure number: the two volumes are in the same unit, so the unit cancels.

blocks.where: L is the stroke in m and N the speed in rev/s; the piston covers two strokes per revolution. Car engines run at 8 to 15 m/s at rated speed.

blocks.text: Mean effective pressure (mep) is the steady pressure that, acting on the piston over one stroke of every cycle, would give the same net work per cycle as the real, changing pressure: mep = Wnet/Vs, with W in J and Vs in m³ giving Pa. Because it divides out the size, it compares a small fast engine with a large slow one on a fair basis.

sections.h3: The parts, their job and their material

blocks.text: Group the parts by job and the list stops feeling long: some hold everything together, some take the gas pressure, some deliver the output, some control the gas flow, and one smooths the rotation.

head: Part
Job
Usual material
rows: Cylinder block
holds the cylinders, coolant jackets and main bearings
grey cast iron; aluminium alloy in light engines
Cylinder liner
a renewable wearing surface for the piston (dry or wet liner)
centrifugally cast iron, often alloyed
Cylinder head
closes the cylinders; carries valves, ports and the spark plug or injector
cast iron or aluminium alloy
Head gasket
seals gas, coolant and oil between head and block
multi-layer steel, or copper and asbestos-free fibre
Piston
takes the gas pressure and passes it to the connecting rod
aluminium-silicon alloy; cast iron in some slow diesels
Piston rings
compression rings seal the gas; the oil ring scrapes oil off the bore
fine-grain cast iron or steel, often chromium plated
Gudgeon pin
hinges the piston to the connecting rod
case-hardened steel
Connecting rod
links the piston to the crank pin
forged carbon or alloy steel
Crankshaft
turns the push of the rods into rotation
forged alloy steel, or spheroidal graphite iron
Main and big-end bearings
carry the crankshaft and rods on an oil film
steel shells lined with white metal or copper-lead
Flywheel
stores energy between power strokes and keeps speed steady
cast iron or steel
Camshaft and valves
open and close the gas passages on time
cam: cast iron or steel; valves: alloy steel, exhaust valve with chromium and silicon
Inlet and exhaust manifolds
carry charge in and burnt gas out
inlet: aluminium or plastic; exhaust: cast iron or steel
Crankcase and oil sump
house the crank and hold the lubricating oil
cast iron, aluminium alloy or pressed steel

blocks.text: Valve timing and the order in which the cylinders fire are separate topics; see valve and port timing diagrams and firing order, valve layouts and valve actuation.

items: The piston reverses direction twice per revolution, so it must be light. Aluminium alloy is about one third as dense as cast iron, so the reversing force stays small; it also carries heat away from the crown quickly.
The crankshaft is twisted by each cylinder in turn and bent by the gas load, millions of times. Forged steel resists this fatigue, and the journals are ground and hardened for the bearings.
The block must be rigid, cheap and good at damping vibration. Cast iron does all three; an aluminium block saves weight but needs iron liners where the piston slides.
The exhaust valve runs red hot. Steel alloyed with chromium and silicon keeps its strength and resists scaling at that temperature.
Rings must press outward on the bore and still slide. Cast iron keeps its springiness when hot, and its graphite helps it slide.

blocks.text: The gap between piston and bore is set for the hot running state, because the aluminium piston expands more than the iron bore. A cold engine on a winter morning therefore makes a little piston slap that disappears once it warms up.

spec.aria: Section of one cylinder with head, two valves and a spark plug, coolant jacket, piston at bottom dead centre with rings and gudgeon pin, connecting rod and crank. Dimension lines show bore 80 millimetres and stroke 90 millimetres; the clearance volume is 62.8 and the swept volume 452.4 cubic centimetres.

examples.question: A four-cylinder engine has a bore of 80 mm, a stroke of 90 mm and a clearance volume of 62.8 cm³ per cylinder. Find the swept volume of one cylinder, the displacement, the compression ratio and the crank radius.
steps: Work in centimetres so the volume comes out in cm³: d = 8.0 cm, L = 9.0 cm.
Swept volume: V<sub>s</sub> = (π/4) d² L = 0.7854 × 64.0 × 9.0 = 452.4 cm³.
Displacement: 4 × 452.4 = 1809.6 cm³, about 1.8 litre, the figure a brochure prints.
examples.answer: V<sub>s</sub> = 452.4 cm³ per cylinder, displacement 1809.6 cm³ (1.8 L), r = 8.20, crank radius 45 mm.

examples.question: The same engine runs at 3000 rev/min with an indicated mean effective pressure of 8 bar. Find the mean piston speed and the indicated power of the engine.
steps: A four-stroke cylinder completes N/2 = 25 cycles per second.
Work per cycle per cylinder: mep × V<sub>s</sub> = 8 × 10⁵ Pa × 452.4 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 361.9 J.
Indicated power: 4 cylinders × 361.9 J × 25 per s = 36 190 W = 36.2 kW.
examples.answer: Mean piston speed 9.0 m/s; indicated power 36.2 kW.

traps: Compression ratio is not V<sub>s</sub>/V<sub>c</sub>. The charge starts in the whole volume at BDC, V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>, and ends in V<sub>c</sub>; the slip gives 7.20 instead of 8.20 in the example.
A bore of 80 mm is 8.0 cm, not 80 cm. Put the bore and the stroke in the same unit before you square and multiply.
Stroke is twice the crank radius, not the crank radius.
Swept volume is one cylinder; displacement is all cylinders. Read which one the question asks for.
mep needs V<sub>s</sub> in m³ to give pascals. Feed it cm³ and the answer is a million times too small.

quiz.q: Define bore and stroke and give the usual unit of each.
quiz.a: Bore is the inside diameter of the cylinder; stroke is the distance the piston moves from TDC to BDC. Both are quoted in mm.

quiz.q: Name the usual material of the piston, the connecting rod and the cylinder block.
quiz.a: Piston: aluminium-silicon alloy. Connecting rod: forged steel. Block: grey cast iron, or aluminium alloy in light engines.

quiz.q: Why is the piston made of aluminium alloy rather than cast iron?
quiz.a: It reverses direction twice per revolution, so its mass sets the inertia force. Aluminium alloy is about one third as dense as cast iron and conducts heat better, so the force and the crown temperature both stay lower.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of piston ring and what does each do?
quiz.a: Compression rings (the top one or two) seal the gas pressure. The oil control ring at the bottom scrapes surplus oil off the bore back to the sump.

quiz.q: A single-cylinder engine has a bore of 100 mm, a stroke of 120 mm and a clearance volume of 100 cm³. Find V<sub>s</sub> and r.
An engine of 1.81 L displacement does 700 J of net indicated work per cycle (all cylinders together). Find the mep in bar.
A student finds r = 452.4/62.8 = 7.20 for the worked example. What went wrong, and which ratio heats the charge more?
quiz.a: The student used V<sub>s</sub>/V<sub>c</sub>; the BDC volume is V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>, so r = 515.2/62.8 = 8.20. The larger ratio squeezes the charge into a relatively smaller space and gives a higher temperature and pressure at the end of compression.

quiz.q: Why can the clearance volume never be zero?
quiz.a: It holds the combustion chamber, the valve heads and the plug or injector tip, and it absorbs the growth of the hot piston and rod. With zero clearance the piston would strike the head, and the compression ratio would be infinite.

beyond: Engine simulation tools build the cylinder model from exactly these numbers: bore, stroke, rod length and clearance volume. Materials keep moving: many blocks are now aluminium with cast-in iron liners or sprayed coatings, and diesel pistons carry steel crowns or a steel insert for the top ring groove. Search for piston ring pack design, plasma-sprayed bores and forged steel pistons.
